issues.title: Update levels of access to technological safeguards
issues.author: maggiedelano
issues.body:
- Instead of “normal” – could this be “high”? Normal implies a common baseline.
- Instead of “impaired” – could we use “limited”? Not having a high-level of access could be due to lack of information/understanding or because of the type of control of the abuser and the inability to use tech safety.

issues.title: Update document to include discussion of specific attacks
issues.author: maggiedelano
issues.body:
Update the threat model to discuss specific attacks on the DULT architecture. This could include:

- Multiple tags following a single victim
- Non-compliant tags (e.g. speaker disabled, altered firmware/firmware updates, spoofed, non-compliant tags)
- Remote advertisement monitoring
- Remote disablement

Each of these attacks may be significant enough to warrant their own issues; this issue will link to those issues if/as they are created.

The document should also include discussion of attacks that are considered out of scope.

issues.title: Discuss possible design tradeoffs
issues.author: maggiedelano
issues.body: Detecting unwanted location tracking is often discussed as a trade off between privacy of unassociated tag owners and security of tracking victims (see e.g. [this article](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1332.pdf)). However, victims could be threatened using either attacks related to [remote advertisement monitoring](https://github.com/ietf-wg-dult/threat-model/issues/17) as well as the "standard" tracking scenario. Update the document to discuss this, and how the protocol should prioritize different types of attacks, victims, etc.

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body:
Pushing this to Post-IETF 122. Relevant section is on line 117 in the current draft:

> It is also appropriate to define who is using the tracking tags and incorporate this into a model. This is because if protocols overly deprioritize the privacy of tracking tags’ users, an attacker could use a victim’s own tag to track them. Beck et al. describe a [possible technological solution](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1332.pdf) to the problem of user privacy vs privacy of other potential victims. In designing the protocol, these concerns should be weighed equally. TODO: Is this actually how we want to weigh them? This warrants further discussion.

Text could also be added to the Privacy and Security Requirements section (currently 4.1.4).

issues.title: Proposal: Address False Positives in Unwanted Tracking Detection
issues.author: shaileshprabhu95
issues.body:
**Summary**:
The draft currently lacks a discussion on false positives in unwanted tracking detection, which can undermine the system’s effectiveness. False alarms reduce user trust, impact legitimate tracking use cases (e.g., shared devices, IoT deployments), and may create legal risks for service providers.

**Key Issues with False Positives**:
1. **Users May Ignore Alerts**: If alerts occur too frequently for legitimate tracking devices, users may start ignoring them, making real tracking threats harder to detect.
2. **Disrupts Enterprise & Shared Spaces**: Workplaces, hospitals, rental cars, and logistics environments rely on Bluetooth tracking for legitimate purposes.
3. **Legal & Compliance Risks**: Misidentification of devices as malicious could create privacy disputes and regulatory challenges.

**Proposed Enhancements:**

1. **Define Common Causes of False Positives**
    - **Legitimate shared devices** (e.g., family members’ AirTags, corporate assets).
    - **Overlapping Bluetooth signals** in crowded areas.
    - **Short-term presence vs. actual tracking threats** (e.g., an AirTag in a borrowed bag vs. malicious tracking).
    - **Algorithmic errors** in motion pattern analysis.

2. **Introduce Heuristic-Based Filtering Mechanisms**
    - **Context Awareness**: Reduce false alerts by factoring in historical interactions with a device.
    - **Adaptive Learning**: Allow user feedback (e.g., "Mark this tracker as trusted").
    - **Risk-Based Confidence Score**: Instead of binary alerts, show a low/medium/high risk score based on tracking duration and proximity.

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body: Addressed in #49.

issues.title: Elaborate on Power Constraints in Threat Model Draft (Section 4.2.2 - Power constraints)
issues.author: shaileshprabhu95
issues.body:
Given that unwanted tracking detection often relies on periodic Bluetooth scanning, continuous background monitoring can significantly impact battery life on mobile devices. The Threat Model draft should explicitly discuss power limitations and propose energy-efficient solutions.

**Proposed Enhancements**
I propose adding the following details to Section 4.2.2 (Power Constraints):

1. **Challenges of Continuous Scanning**:
    - Constantly scanning for tracking devices drains the battery, making detection mechanisms impractical for everyday use.
    - High-frequency scanning increases energy consumption, especially on mobile devices with limited battery capacity.

2. **Potential Power-Efficient Approaches**:
    - **Adaptive Scanning**: Dynamically adjust the scan frequency based on detected risk levels (e.g., increase frequency when a suspicious device is nearby).
    - **Event-Triggered Detection**: Activate scanning only when the user enters a high-risk scenario (e.g., when moving into a new location or after a prolonged stationary period).
    - **Low-Power Mode for Background Detection**: Use low-energy techniques such as passive Bluetooth listening instead of active scanning.
    - **Offloading Detection to Edge Devices**: Explore offloading detection tasks to companion devices (e.g., smartwatches or home hubs) to distribute power consumption.

3. **Impact on Protocol Design**:
    - The DULT protocol must balance **detection accuracy** with **battery efficiency** to ensure usability.
    - Consideration of **device-specific power constraints** (e.g., differences between smartphones, wearables, and IoT devices).

issues.title: Proposal to elaborate on Device Constraints (Section 4.2.3)
issues.author: shaileshprabhu95
issues.body:
The draft currently has a placeholder for **Device Constraints (Section 4.2.3)** under **Design Constraints**. This section may explicitly outline hardware, OS, processing, and connectivity limitations that impact unwanted tracking detection.

**Proposed Additions**
1. **Hardware Limitations**
    - Variability in BLE scanning capabilities across older vs. newer smartphones, feature phones, and IoT devices.
    - Differences in antenna sensitivity, chipset power, and OS-level access impacting detection.

2. **OS and Platform Restrictions**
    - Mobile OS restrictions on background BLE scanning (e.g., iOS/Android privacy policies).
    - Wearables and IoT devices may have stricter power and resource limitations.
  
3. **Processing and Memory Constraints**
    - Limited processing power and RAM on low-end devices can make continuous tracking detection difficult.
    - Some ML-based detection mechanisms may be too resource-intensive for constrained devices.

4. **Connectivity and Cloud Dependency**
    - Some tracking detection approaches rely on cloud services, which may not work in offline or low-connectivity environments.
    - Devices in airplane mode, rural areas, or secure environments may not have access to cloud-assisted detection.

**Potential Enhancements**
- Introduce lightweight detection mechanisms for constrained devices.
- Define adaptive scanning strategies based on device capabilities.
- Discuss fallback mechanisms when a device lacks full detection capability.

comments.body: Thanks for the suggestion! Feel free to make a PR. I'd expand a bit on these points to follow the format we have been using (short paragraphs rather than bullets), and flesh it out a little bit (e.g. which concrete privacy policies that need to be considered?)

issues.title: Adding BLE Constraints Section to Design Constraints
issues.author: shaileshprabhu95
issues.body:
Given that unwanted tracking detection heavily relies on **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)** technology, it is important to outline the protocol's inherent limitations that impact detection mechanisms. Adding this section will strengthen the draft by explicitly acknowledging BLE’s constraints and ensuring detection mechanisms are designed with these limitations in mind.

**Proposed Additions:**
The new section should cover:

1. **Packet Size Limitations**:
    - BLE advertisement packets have a maximum payload size of 31 bytes in legacy advertisements (Bluetooth 4.0/4.1/4.2).
    - Bluetooth 5.0+ introduces extended advertisements with a higher payload capacity of 255 bytes, but not all devices support this feature.
    - These limitations constrain the amount of metadata that can be included in advertisements for unwanted tracking detection.
    
2. **Nature of Public Advertisements**:
    - BLE advertisements are typically public and can be passively scanned by any nearby receiver, which raises privacy concerns.
    - Devices implementing unwanted tracking detection must balance open detection with privacy-preserving mechanisms to avoid unnecessary exposure.

3. **Broadcast Interval Trade-offs**:
    - BLE advertisements are transmitted at specific intervals, impacting detection latency.
    - Frequent advertisements improve tracking accuracy but increase power consumption.
    - Adaptive strategies are required to optimize both efficiency and detection reliability.

4. **Protocol-Level Constraints**:
    - BLE operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, making it susceptible to interference from Wi-Fi, microwave ovens, and other wireless devices.
    - Some BLE devices implement privacy features (randomized MAC addresses), which may hinder persistent tracking.
    - The BLE stack on mobile OS platforms (iOS/Android) imposes background scanning limitations, affecting continuous monitoring.

issues.title: Remote disablement is underspecified
issues.author: bledvina
issues.body: Reading section 3.2.6 entitled Misuse of Remote Disablement, I don't think "Remote Disablement" is defined sufficiently well. The first sentence explains how an "attacker might misuse remote disablement features," but then the third sentence talks about "The ability to disable a victim's protections." I think defining what remote disablement means in the context of this document would help. For example, it could be remote disablement of location tracking or it could be remote disablement of unwanted tracking protections or both or it could mean something else entirely.

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body:
Thanks Brent, I think being more specific is a good idea. As you've said, it could have to do with disablement of location tracking or unwanted tracking protections only, and I'd add that this could be done on the tracking tag or the device. 

I think @exploretechsafety was working on this section, so I'll give them a chance to respond as well and see if we can clarify the text. I don't think we will get this in by the deadline at 23:59 UTC today, but if we can come to consensus before the meeting we will have time to discuss other topics.

issues.title: Rotating Tracker IDs
issues.author: bledvina
issues.body: I see two potential issues with the Rotating Tracker IDs section (Section 3.27). The first is that this section appears to be a subset of the Non-compliant tags section (Section 3.2.5). The second issue is that rotating tracker IDs are not inherently a problem. Nominally, you want the static information in the BT payload to rotate periodically to minimize local privacy concerns but also balance longer-term unwanted tracking detection.  Is the Rotating Tracker IDs section meant to state that an attacker being able to rotate tracker IDs too fast (e.g., once per minute) is the problem?

I'd guess the issue is more someone rotating tracker IDs too fast, @shaileshprabhu95 was the one who did the first draft of this section, so I'll let them comment before making changes. As with the other issue, we probably won't be able to fix in the next few hours, but would be good to try to come to consensus before the next meeting.

issues.author: bledvina
issues.body:
I have a couple concerns with Section 3.2.4 (Remote Advertisement Monitoring). First, BT advertisements can be received whether they are encrypted or not. Maybe the point is that they cannot be decoded when encrypted? Irrespective, it's not clear why encryption matters here.

The second concern I have is the last sentence in this section calls out use of advanced correlation techniques, and I think I understand what is meant, but it might be helpful to explain in more detail or provide a reference.

1) How about changing the first sentence in that section from "Bluetooth advertisement packets are not encrypted, so any device with Bluetooth scanning capabilities in proximity to a location tracking tag can receive Bluetooth advertisement packets." to "Any device with Bluetooth scanning capabilities in proximity to a location tracking tag can receive Bluetooth advertisement packets."

issues.title: Bluetooth vs other technologies section
issues.author: bledvina
issues.body:
The second sentence in Bluetooth vs other technologies makes a statement that the threat analysis focuses on location tracking tags that use Bluetooth or other technologies. Is this meant to suggest using other technologies than Bluetooth for crowd-sourcing?

Additionally, this section states in the last sentence: "able to transmit its location to other consumer devices." This is one way crowd-sourcing can work, but the alternative way is for a consumer device to transmit its own location as the proxy for the tag's location.

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body:
I think we went back and forth on this a bit at the last meeting (about how broadly to define the scope of the document with respect to Bluetooth vs. other techniques). I agree we should try to be precise here. Maybe we can clarify this phrase "if a tag were designed using a technology other than Bluetooth" to something like "if a tag were designed **for crowd-sourced location tracking** using a technology other than Bluetooth"? Tagging @exploretechsafety as I think they wrote this section.

For the last sentence, what about something like "able to participate in a crowd-sourced location tracking network"? We can try to use the same wording for both parts, and eventually aligning with the other documents (see also #34).

issues.title: Spoofing Legitimate Devices section
issues.author: bledvina
issues.body:
I'm not sure I follow what is covered in this section. Crowd-sourcing networks typically look for certain types of Bluetooth advertisements, not common Bluetooth devices. Given that, it's not clear how modifying a tracker to mimic a common Bluetooth device would be a threat.

Additionally, another spoofing scenario worth calling out is recording and replaying Bluetooth advertisements from a legitimate tracker. This is generally straightforward and presents challenges on attribution.

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body: Thanks, Brent. I think the key here would be spoofing a device that is then able to participate in the crowd-sourced location tracking network. We should also include the other spoofing scenario you mentioned. @shaileshprabhu95 can you take a look here as well and propose some changes?

pulls.title: Adding Threat Matrix and additional Threats to Section 3.3 and Section 3.2 respectively of draft-ietf-dult-threat-model
pulls.author: shaileshprabhu95
pulls.body:
This PR adds:

1. Additional threats to Section 3.2
2. Introducing a Threat Matrix in Section 3.3

comments.author: shaileshprabhu95
comments.body:
Hi Maggie,

Thank you for the review. I have updated this PR to incorporate your feedback. The revisions include:

1. Adding descriptions for the impact, likelihood, feasibility, and risk levels that were removed from the Threat Matrix headers.
2. Expanding the attack profiles with additional details on how each attack works, its feasibility, and its impact.
3. Defining "Mitigation Available" and providing definitions for the other columns as well.

Please review the updated PR and let me know if any further refinements are needed. Thanks! @maggiedelano

comments.author: shaileshprabhu95
comments.body:
Hi Maggie,

Thanks for reviewing it further and adding suggestions. I have addressed your review comments in the latest commit with the below modifications:

1. I've rephrased the risk statements to explicitly consider **impact**, **likelihood**, and **feasibility** in a balanced manner.
2. The attacks with the same inputs have the same risk score. Each attack now follows the below logical pattern:
    - High Impact + High Likelihood + Easy Feasibility → High Risk
    - High Impact + Medium Likelihood + Moderate/Hard Feasibility → Medium Risk
    - Medium Impact + Medium Likelihood + Moderate Feasibility → Medium Risk
3. I've moved the threat matrix and table to the beginning of the section.

Please review and let me know if you need further refinements. Thanks! @maggiedelano

comments.author: maggiedelano
comments.body: Fixed some minor formatting issues, merging now.

reviews.author: maggiedelano
reviews.body:
Thanks for your PR!

I made some minor commits, fixing the trailing white space, and also truncating the column headers because they were too long to fit the HTML view appropriately.

I think a few additions would be helpful:
1. Adding the low/medium/high descriptions to the text since they were removed from the headers
2. We should discuss the profile of each attack in a bit more detail in each of the paragraphs now that we have the table. This reasoning will also help me and others assess whether each cell in the matrix is appropriate or not.
3. Can you define what you mean by mitigation available? (And if it makes sense, the definitions of any of the other columns)

If you can take a first pass at this, that would be great, and I can help update further as needed.

reviews.author: maggiedelano
reviews.body:
Thanks for the updates!

I think this is pretty close.

Some minor suggestions:
- It is a little confusing to phrase the risk as "The X feasibility makes this a Y" risk attack. Could you rephrase those? Some phrase that considers both impact, likelihood and feasibility. e.g. The risk is high due to a high impact that is moderately feasible and likely.
- I'd also make sure you double check so that any attacks with the same inputs have the same risk score.
- Can you move the threat matrix and table to the beginning of this section? Since we discuss them in the attack paragraphs it would be helpful for the definitions to be there.

Thanks!
